shortDescription: In Edessa and Nisibis, between the Roman and Persian empires, Christians who spoke Syriac sang their teaching in Ephrem's hymns. Among them were men and women vowed to live unmarried and holy for God.

timeline.headline: A flood at Edessa destroys the Christians' church
timeline.witness: The Chronicle of Edessa, whose last entries fall under the emperor Justinian, from the city's own records

lines.when: November of "the year 513" of the Greeks
lines.text: After a great and violent rain in the night, the river breaks down Edessa's western wall. King Abgar watches the water by torchlight from a tower. The flood overthrows his palace, destroys the temple of the church of the Christians, and kills more than two thousand people, many of them asleep.
The city's scribes record the flood and the king's command, and the keepers of the archives store the record.

timeline.headline: Tatian weaves one Gospel story from the four, and Edessa's founding story pictures it read

lines.text: Tatian, who says he was born in the land of the Assyrians, makes a combination of the Gospels he calls the Diatessaron. Eusebius says it is still in the hands of some.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IV.29.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 26424-26433, 26479; Tatian, Address to the Greeks 42, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 7458-7461
lines.note: Eusebius wrote in the fourth century.

lines.text: The Doctrine of Addai, Edessa's founding story, pictures a great crowd gathering each day for prayer and for the reading of the Old and New Testament and of the Diatessaron.
lines.reference: Doctrine of Addai, cic/texts/addai_doctrine-of-addai.txt line 65, with the editor's note on the word, line 219
lines.note: A later legend, set in the time of the apostles.

timeline.when: "the six hundred and forty-eighth year" of Alexander
timeline.headline: Aphrahat, a teacher in Persia, writes to the men and women vowed to God

lines.when: "the six hundred and forty-eighth year" of Alexander
lines.text: Aphrahat writes the first ten of his letters.
The church's preachers warn the whole covenant before baptism. Some young men and women choose for themselves a life unmarried and holy, and those who mean to marry are to marry before baptism.
lines.reference: Aphrahat, Demonstration VII.20-21, cic/texts/aphrahat_demonstrations-2-7_hallock1932.txt line 57; Latin, cic/texts/aphrahat_demonstrationes-1-22-syr-lat_parisot1894.txt lines 21939-21942

lines.text: Their Syriac name means sons of the covenant: those who vowed themselves to God to keep from marriage.
lines.note: The editor's explanation of the word.

lines.text: Aphrahat writes that the vowed keep watch and sing psalms and pray, give their goods to the poor, and live apart from the other sex. A vowed man who wants a vowed woman to live with him should rather marry openly.
He gives a daughter of the covenant the words to answer a vowed man who asks her to live with him and serve him: she is promised to a royal husband, and serves him.
lines.reference: Aphrahat, Demonstration VI.7, cic/texts/npnf213_gregory-great-ephraim-syrus-aphrahat.xml lines 25948-25953; Latin, cic/texts/aphrahat_demonstrationes-1-22-syr-lat_parisot1894.txt lines 18126-18134

timeline.headline: At Nisibis, Ephrem teaches in hymns while the Persians besiege the city

lines.text: Nisibis lies on the border between Persia and Rome.
lines.note: Theodoret wrote about a century later.

lines.text: Ephrem, though he had no schooling, becomes learned in the language of the Syrians.
lines.note: Sozomen wrote in the next century.

lines.text: Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, dies.
lines.note: The old sources differ on whether Jacob lived through the siege.

lines.text: In a hymn for the siege, Ephrem sets the river that threatens the city beside Noah's flood, after which God set his bow over the earth as a promise. Its refrain asks God to stretch out his bow against the flood that has lifted its waves against the walls.
He asks Christ, who rose on the third day, not to give the city over to death in its third peril.

Theodoret says the Persians dammed the river and broke the walls with its water, that Jacob prayed inside the church while the walls were built up again, and that at Ephrem's request he called down clouds of mosquitoes and gnats on the army.
lines.note: Theodoret's account, written about a century later. The wonders are his.

lines.text: In a hymn on the bishops of Nisibis, Ephrem says the city's first priest, dead and buried within her, became a wall around her.

timeline.headline: The king of Persia turns on its Christians
timeline.witness: Sozomen, a Greek church historian of the next century

lines.text: As the Christians grow in number, form churches and appoint priests and deacons, the Magi, the priests who guard the Persian religion, are deeply angered.

Shapur believes a charge that the bishop, Symeon, is a friend of the Roman emperor. He taxes the Christians heavily, hoping want will make them give up their faith, then orders their priests killed and their churches pulled down.
In the Syriac acts of the Persian martyrs, the king says that Simon wants to make his people servants of the emperor, who shares their faith.
lines.reference: Acts of the Persian martyrs, German tr. Braun, cic/texts/persian-martyr-acts_ausgewahlte-akten-persischer-martyrer-bkv22-deu_braun1915.txt lines 1575-1578
lines.note: The king's words, as the Christian acts report them.

lines.text: Sozomen counts sixteen thousand men and women martyred in this time whose names are known, with a multitude beyond counting, and says the people of Edessa took great care over their names.

timeline.when: "the six hundred and fifty-fifth year" of the Greeks
timeline.headline: Aphrahat writes of the persecution

lines.when: "the six hundred and fifty-fifth year" of the Greeks
lines.text: Aphrahat writes his last twelve letters, in the thirty-fifth year of the Persian king.
He is vexed by a reproach: if they have a God, why does he not avenge his people?
In his own day, he writes, many declare their faith and are killed.

timeline.headline: Rome hands Nisibis to Persia, and Ephrem moves to Edessa

lines.text: The new emperor, his army in danger of starving inside Persia, makes peace and gives up Nisibis.
lines.note: Socrates wrote in the next century.

lines.text: When Nisibis is handed to the Persians, Ephrem withdraws to Edessa, where he spends the rest of his life and opens a school.
lines.reference: Barhadbeshabba, Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, cic/texts/barhadbeshabba_cause-de-la-fondation-des-ecoles-po4-syr-fra_scher1908.txt lines 20435-20438
lines.note: Barhadbeshabba wrote more than two centuries later.

lines.text: In prose, Ephrem answers three rival teachers: Marcion, who taught a Stranger God apart from the Maker; Mani, who taught two Roots; and Bardaisan, who taught five Entities set in empty space. Their works and their fast are like ours, he writes, but their faith is not.
lines.note: Ephrem's own words, the rivals as he tells them.

lines.text: Sozomen says Ephrem, afraid the Syrians would take up the opinions in the songs of Bardaisan's son Harmonius, wrote hymns to the same tunes by the church's teaching, and from then on the Syrians sang his hymns.
lines.note: Sozomen wrote in the next century.

lines.when: the ninth of June, "the year 684" of the Greeks
lines.text: Ephrem dies. Palladius calls him the deacon of the church of Edessa.
lines.reference: Chronicle of Edessa 30, cic/texts/chronicle-of-edessa_cowper.txt line 103; Palladius, Lausiac History 40, cic/texts/palladius_lausiac-history_clarke1918.txt line 471

timeline.when: In the 11th year of King Yazdegerd's reign
timeline.headline: A later Persian king lets the churches rebuild, and forty bishops meet in synod
timeline.witness: The acts of the synod of Mar Isaac, in Chabot's French

lines.text: Socrates says the Roman emperor sent Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia, on a mission to the king of the Persians, who then let him build churches wherever he wished.
lines.note: Socrates wrote a generation later. The wonders he tells of Maruthas are left out here.

lines.when: in the 11th year of King Yazdegerd's reign
lines.text: The king has ordered the churches his fathers destroyed to be rebuilt, the prisoners freed, and "the priests, the leaders and all the holy covenant" to go about freely and without fear.
This came about, the acts say, in the time of Mar Isaac, through the work of the bishop Marutha, the go-between of peace and concord between East and West, and of the bishops of the Romans.

lines.when: at the feast of the Epiphany
lines.text: The king orders Isaac and Marutha to gather the bishops in the great church of the capital. The day they meet is for them like the dead rising.
Forty bishops accept the letter sent from the West: one bishop to a city, no longer two or three, and the feasts kept together.
Hosea, bishop of Nisibis, Ephrem's old city, is named second metropolitan, and signs third, after Isaac and Marutha.

timeline.headline: The name of the covenant lasts

lines.text: John of Ephesus still writes of women becoming readers and daughters of the covenant.
lines.reference: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints, cic/texts/john-ephesus_lives-eastern-saints-po17_brooks1923.txt lines 14150-14153
lines.note: John wrote in the sixth century.

uncertain: Whether Bishop Jacob lived through the siege. Theodoret, writing about a century later, says the Persians dammed the river Mygdonius and broke the walls with its water, that Jacob prayed inside the church while the walls were built up again, and that at Ephrem's request he climbed a tower and called down mosquitoes and gnats on the army; the wonders are his. Ephrem's own hymn on the bishops of Nisibis says the city's first priest was already "dead and buried within her," his body a wall for the city. The Chronicle of Edessa puts Jacob's death in the year 649 of the Greeks, 337 or 338.
The year of the siege. Ephrem's hymn calls it the city's "third peril" and gives no year.
The year of the flood. The Chronicle of Edessa sets it in November of the year 513 of the Greeks, which is 201. The translator's notes give 202, and say that Dionysius places the flood in 216.

Why the king turned on the Christians of Persia. Sozomen says the Magi were angered when the Christians grew in number, formed churches and appointed priests and deacons, and that the king believed a charge that their bishop was a friend of the Roman emperor. The Syriac acts of the Persian martyrs put the king's reason in his own mouth: that the bishop would make his people servants of the emperor, who shared their faith.

The one-story Gospel. Only Edessa's late founding story, the Doctrine of Addai, has these churches reading the Diatessaron, and no old line places it at Nisibis or across the whole period. The word itself is the St Petersburg manuscript's reading, which confirms the first editor's guess at an unclear word.

The covenant in 410. The synod's acts use the same word for those the king freed, but the editor of the acts reads it there as the whole clergy, monks included, so it is not shown to be the same vowed order Aphrahat wrote for.
Ephrem's birthplace. Sozomen says he was "a native of Nisibis, or his family was of the neighboring territory."

Why the later king changed course. The acts of 410 say his grant came about in the time of Mar Isaac, through the work of the bishop Marutha, the go-between of peace and concord between East and West, and of the bishops of the Romans. Socrates, a generation later, has the Roman emperor send Maruthas to the Persian king. No old line gives the king's own reason, and the acts do not say whether East and West mean the two empires or the two churches.

quotationOriginals.modern: I am promised in marriage to a royal husband, and I serve him. If I leave his service and serve you, my bridegroom will be angry with me. He will write me a letter of divorce and send me away from his house.
quotationOriginals.printed: To a royal husband am I betrothed, and Him do I serve; and if I leave His service and serve thee, my betrothed will be wroth with me, and will write me a letter of divorce, and will send me away from His house
quotationOriginals.work: Aphrahat, Demonstration VI (Of Monks), section 7, tr. A. E. Johnston (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, 13)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Johnston's English. The Syriac is held only in unreadable scan text. Parisot's Latin of the Syriac (lines 18130-18134) confirms the reading, and its Sponsus meus gives "my bridegroom" for "my betrothed"; the scan runs three of its words together.

quotationOriginals.modern: Stretch out your bow against the flood, for see, it has lifted up its waves against our walls!
quotationOriginals.printed: Stretch forth Thy bow against the flood, for lo! it has lifted up its waves against our walls!
quotationOriginals.work: Ephrem the Syrian, Nisibene Hymn I, refrain, tr. J. T. Sarsfield Stopford (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, 13)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Stopford's English; the Syriac is not held in a readable print. The print marks the line R., for the refrain.

quotationOriginals.modern: Their works are like our works, just as their fast is like our fast, but their faith is not like our faith.
quotationOriginals.printed: For their works are like our works as their fast is like our fast, but their faith is not like our Faith
quotationOriginals.work: Ephrem the Syrian, Prose Refutations, Fifth Discourse to Hypatius, conclusion, tr. C. W. Mitchell (1912)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Mitchell's English; the Syriac is not transcribed in the held file. The palimpsest has gaps nearby, but this sentence is whole in the print.
